detail:
NINDS describes restless legs syndrome (RLS), also known as Willis-Ekbom disease, as a neurological condition that causes an irresistible urge to move the legs. It is classified both as a sleep disorder, because symptoms are triggered by resting and attempting to sleep, and as a movement condition, because people move their legs to find relief. Sensations can include aching, throbbing, pulling, itching, crawling, or creeping, typically appearing after rest, easing with movement, and worsening in the evening and at night, which can make falling and staying asleep difficult.

In most cases the cause is unknown, although NINDS notes that RLS often runs in families and that specific gene variants are associated with the condition. Low levels of iron in the brain may also be responsible, and the condition may be related to dysfunction in the basal ganglia, the part of the brain that controls movement and uses the chemical dopamine. RLS can also occur alongside conditions such as end-stage kidney disease, nerve damage, and pregnancy. There is no single diagnostic test; clinicians review symptoms, medical history, medications, and family history, and blood tests can help rule out contributors such as low iron.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about restless legs syndrome symptoms and diagnosis.
sourceName: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke
summary: NINDS explains restless legs syndrome as a neurological sleep and movement condition causing an irresistible urge to move the legs, with uncomfortable sensations that appear at rest, ease with movement, and worsen at night.
takeaways: an irresistible urge to move the legs is the hallmark symptom
symptoms can include crawling or creeping sensations that worsen at night
low brain iron and family history are among the factors sources describe
title: Restless Legs Syndrome: the urge to move that disrupts sleep
